Q: What does ubuntu-latest mean for GitHub Actions? A:

The ubuntu-latest GitHub runner is a virtual machine on Azure cloud with the latest version of the Ubuntu operating system that is supported by GitHub (24.04 as of February 2026, whereas the latest Ubuntu release is 25.10, see https://releases.ubuntu.com/).

From the GitHub docs:

The -latest runner images are the latest stable images that GitHub provides, and might not be the most recent version of the operating system available from the operating system vendor.

Here's the full specs of the Ubuntu 24.04 GitHub runner image: https://github.com/actions/runner-images/blob/main/images/ubuntu/Ubuntu2404-Readme.md

The table of the currently supported runners is in the repo https://github.com/actions under https://github.com/actions/runner-images:

The Ubuntu images come with grep, find, which (preinstalled-software-for-github-owned-images) as well as recent versions of popular tools such as Java, Node, Go, Python, etc. pre-installed and the standard runner has 2 CPUs / 8GB RAM for private) and 4 CPUs / 16GB RAM for public repositories.

I recommend checking the table with the available images as I recently had a surprise using ubuntu-latest for running my Google Colab notebooks since Colab is still using Ubuntu 22.04 and ubuntu-latest is now 24.04 (and I was installing the latest version of a software that does not provide a build for 22.04).

Q: Switch focus between editor and integrated terminal A:

If you don't want open/close of terminal, below will toggle to focus between editor and terminal with one keybinding:

  1. Open Keyboard Shortcuts

  2. Find first command with typing terminal.focus, change to Shift + T (or whatever you prefer)

  1. Find second command with typing workbench.action.focusActiveEditorGroup, change to Shift + T

Don't forget to change condition terminalFocus

Q: Merging the headers then concatenate the records of a huge number of text files A:

Regarding the second problem - Argument list too long is a shell error message, not an awk one, and the usual solution is to have awk read the list of files from the input rather than passing them as arguments, e.g. using the builtin version of printf as it can't have that argument list size problem:

printf '%s\n' input*.vcf |
awk '
    BEGIN {
        while ( (getline file < ARGV[1]) > 0 ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = file
        }
    }
    ...
' -

If your input looks like this:

$ head input*.vcf
==> input1.vcf <==
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
chrom1 ...
chrom2 ...
...

==> input2.vcf <==
##fileformat=foo
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
this ...
that ...
...

then maybe something like this is what you're looking for, using any awk:

$ cat tst.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

awk '
    BEGIN {
        while ( (getline file < ARGV[1]) > 0 ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = file
        }
        ARGV[1] = "pass=1"
        numFiles = ARGC-1
        ARGV[ARGC++] = "pass=2"
        for ( i=2; i<=numFiles; i++ ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = ARGV[i]
        }
    }
    FNR == 1  { endOfHdrs = 0 }
    (pass == 1) && !endOfHdrs
    (pass == 2) && endOfHdrs
    /^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1 }
' <(printf '%s\n' input*.vcf)


$ ./tst.sh
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
##fileformat=foo
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
chrom1 ...
chrom2 ...
...
this ...
that ...
...

Change ^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1 } to ^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1; if (pass==1) nextfile } or similar if necessary for improved performance.

Q: How can I create a DB for MongoDB container on start up? A:

No need to create a database in advance (they're created on the fly), but it makes sense to create a non-root user the first time the container starts.

docker-compose.yml:

services:
  ...
  mongo:
    image: mongo:6-jammy
    env_file: [.env-mongo, .env]
    volumes:
      - mongo:/data/db
      - ./init-mongo.js:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-mongo.js
      # - ./init-mongo.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-mongo.sh  # mongo < 6

volumes:
  mongo:

init-mongo.sh doesn't need to be executable. It's sourced.

.env (app's variables):

MONGO_USER=user
MONGO_PASSWORD=userpasswd
MONGO_DB=foo

.env-mongo (mongo service's variables):

MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=root
MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=rootpasswd
MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE=foo  # for mongo >= 6

Since mongo-6 one can use process.env, so use init-mongo.js. Before that, use init-mongo.sh (change the script that you attach in docker-compose.yml, and MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE is not needed in this case).

.env is meant to be used by the app service(s), .env-mongo by the mongo service.

MONGO_INITDB_* variables are used by the mongo's entrypoint. The docs can be found on Docker Hub. Also it's the entrypoint that runs the initialization script.

init-mongo.js:

db.getSiblingDB('admin').auth(
    process.env.MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME,
    process.env.MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD
);
db.createUser({
    user: process.env.MONGO_USER,
    pwd: process.env.MONGO_PASSWORD,
    roles: ["readWrite"],
});

init-mongo.sh:

q_MONGO_USER=`jq --arg v "$MONGO_USER" -n '$v'`
q_MONGO_PASSWORD=`jq --arg v "$MONGO_PASSWORD" -n '$v'`
mongo -u "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME" -p "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" admin <<EOF
    use foo;
    db.createUser({
        user: $q_MONGO_USER,
        pwd: $q_MONGO_PASSWORD,
        roles: ["readWrite"],
    });
EOF
